content.title: College Basketball Crown Imposes Strict Team Promo Requirements
content.text: Skip to main content Home Leagues College Sports College Basketball Crown Imposes Strict Team Promo Requirements The postseason tournament, now in its second season, has established clearly defined PR objectives for participating teams within their contracts. Design by Sportico, Photo by Louis Grasse/Getty Images The College Basketball Crown, the second-year postseason men’s basketball tournament produced by AEG and Fox—will tip off its second edition on April Fool’s Day in Las Vegas, as organizers look to bolster the event’s relevance following a debut that struggled to attract marquee programs. After fielding 16 teams last year, the Crown has scaled back to eight for 2026: Oklahoma, Colorado, Stanford, West Virginia, Baylor, Minnesota, Rutgers and Creighton. And the tournament is leaning heavily on those participating programs to drive visibility and fan engagement. An addendum to team agreements outlines 14 highly specific marketing requirements—far more prescriptive than the general promotional language typically found in college sports event contracts. According to a copy of Minnesota’s agreement, obtained by Sportico through a records request, the school was required to send a dedicated email promoting ticketing and travel packages within 24 hours after being announced as a participant. Within 48 hours, it was to follow up with a separate email highlighting travel and lodging details, as well as information about the event’s “Circa Stadium Swim Fan Fest.” The contract also mandates a coordinated social medial push, where schools had to publish at least one post on the their team’s primary Instagram, X and Facebook accounts, along with corresponding story posts. For each round the team advances to, it must make an additional social post that includes a “call to action to buy tickets.” Within 12 hours of the team’s flight departure, it must publicly announce the roster of players traveling to Las Vegas. Beyond marketing, Minnesota is obligated to purchase 50 tickets from VividSeats—another partner—for each session it plays in, at total costs of $2,079 for the first round, and $2,599 for the semifinals and championships. In return, the tournament agrees to cover the team’s travel expenses, including charter flights via JSX, and to reimburse the teams for a food and beverage allowance of $4,500. Minnesota’s agreement stems from an overarching term sheet the Crown and Big Ten Conference signed in 2024; the league has a preexisting relationship with Fox. While the event is promoting a $500,000 prize pool—with the winning program receiving $300,000—those figures are not referenced on the agreement with Minnesota. The Crown is seeking to establish itself in a college basketball postseason landscape upended by NIL and the transfer portal.
